extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners interested in the history and practice of peer review and scholarly publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize historical development, practices, and evaluative dimensions of peer review used in scholarly journals and grant review. Useful for understanding how different review practices affect quality, legitimacy, and reform debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external referees (external refereeing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Soliciting written reports from expert referees outside the editorial office to advise editors about submitted papers or proposals; became more systematic in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically optional and used when editors wanted help justifying rejection or when workload increased; external refereeing became more common post-WWII as journals and funders sought outside expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial judgment versus refereeing
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions made by an editor or editorial staff based on their own authority instead of sending submissions to outside referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial journals and dynamic editors often preferred editorial control for speed and to recruit content; lack of formal refereeing did not prevent such journals from publishing important work in earlier periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee role: adviser versus gatekeeper
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether referees are expected merely to advise editors about obvious problems or to act as gatekeepers responsible for the overall quality of the scientific literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the mid-19th century referees primarily advised editors (flagging embarrassing or discrediting content); as concerns about literature quality grew, referees increasingly were seen as gatekeepers, concentrating power among elite reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and confidentiality of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping referee identities secret from authors (and sometimes the public) to promote candid feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defended as necessary for candidness (e.g., NSF response to Congressional scrutiny); contested in reform debates (calls for signed reports to increase accountability and thoughtfulness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and selection of 'peers' (narrowness of reviewer pool)
rubrics_metrics.description: Who counts as an acceptable reviewer — the term 'peer review' implies a narrow range of expert colleagues eligible to evaluate work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The shift in terminology from 'refereeing' to 'peer review' limited the acceptable reviewers to close disciplinary peers, shaping whose judgments were considered legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and logistical constraints (speed versus review thoroughness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The trade-off between rapid publication schedules and time-consuming refereeing procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial journals with regular schedules prioritized speed and content recruitment, making extensive external refereeing impractical; editors sometimes avoided refereeing to keep publication timely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review as marker of scientific legitimacy and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which peer review signals that research is trustworthy, rigorous, and deserving of publication or funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gained prominence during the Cold War as governments and the public demanded accountability; scientists used peer review to claim intellectual autonomy and to convince funders and legislators of responsible decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and bias in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns that peer review may produce systematic unfairness, including gender, racial/ethnic, nepotistic, or other biases in referee reports and funding/publication outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies (e.g., Wennerås & Wold; Ginther et al.) indicate disparities in outcomes; critiques argue peer review can disadvantage women and underrepresented minorities and can reflect favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of peer review in discriminating good and bad science
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether peer review actually distinguishes high-quality research from poor or fraudulent work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics point to high-profile examples of flawed or fraudulent papers that passed review and to studies questioning peer review's efficacy; official reviews have concluded there is limited solid evidence on its overall effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and reform options (signed reports, open review, community feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals and experiments to increase openness in review, such as having referees sign reports, publishing reports, or relying on community-wide feedback (e.g., arXiv).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates argue signing increases accountability and constructiveness; alternatives include open posting for community comment or other models (so far few reforms have been widely adopted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective referee decision-making (consensus models like eLife)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures where multiple referees and the editor discuss a submission together to produce a single, unified decision rather than independent reports sent to the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: eLife's approach: solicits opinions but has referees and editors discuss to arrive at one unanimous decision; this reduces conflicting reports being passed verbatim to authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between journal review and grant/funding review
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct practices and expectations for evaluating journal articles versus grant proposals, including the use of in-house panels, external referees, and differing emphases in evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many funding bodies historically used in-house evaluations or small trusted committees; some funders adopted external referees to promote fairness, while others resisted outside input for reasons of speed or control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal society vetting versus external refereeing
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes where learned societies used internal, often non-anonymous vetting to protect the society's reputation versus open solicitation of external reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal review aimed to ensure publications bore well on the society and to prevent seditious or heretical content; these practices did not map directly onto modern anonymous external refereeing systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical contingency and adaptability of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that the form, purpose, and centrality of peer review have shifted over time according to the needs of scientific communities and their funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review has been reshaped by needs such as establishing credibility, improving literature quality, and assuring patrons; this contingency suggests the system is not immutable and can be reformed.
